title: Freya and the Hymn
premise: Xanthe Eastwick, a property surveyor with a compulsive habit of documenting everything, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House on the eve of the harvest moon. The house responds to his measurements — rooms shift, walls breathe, and his notes rewrite themselves — and waiting on the porch is Wren, the imaginary friend he invented at age seven, unchanged while Xanthe has grown old enough to forget him. As Xanthe digs through the house's ledgers he discovers that every previous surveyor was 'invited in' as a vessel for something the founding family harvested under the full moon, and that Wren is not a memory but the previous vessel, wearing a child's shape. To survive until sunrise Xanthe must choose between destroying the documentation that anchors him to reality or completing it — because the house can only take what cannot prove it was ever someone else. He ends the night by signing the deed over to himself, becoming the house's new keeper, and locking Wren — and the truth of what he invited in at age seven — inside forever.
about_author: Vesper Joubert is the pen name of a former land registry clerk from coastal Maine who spent eleven years cataloguing deeds to houses that no longer exist. Their fiction explores the terror of paperwork done perfectly.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Order
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. A routine assignment arrives: Hollowmere House, vacant forty years, appraisal due before month's end. We learn Xanthe's ritual — photographs, measurements, marginalia — and how documentation steadies him since a childhood he barely remembers. Emotional beat: quiet unease beneath professional calm; the reader senses the order itself is a defense.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. First approach to the house at dusk: it is too symmetrical, its windows arranged like a face mid-blink. His laser measure returns impossible numbers — hallway lengths that differ on each pass. He documents anyway, because writing it down makes it real. Emotional beat: the thrill of an anomaly curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. On the wraparound porch sits a small boy in outdated clothes, patient as furniture. He says, 'You came back,' and calls himself Wren. Xanthe's body remembers before his mind does — the games, the rules, the promises. Emotional beat: vertigo of recognition; grief disguised as nostalgia.

chapters.title: Rules of Play
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Wren explains the game they used to play: hide-and-seek, but the seeker must never stop counting. Xanthe realizes the counting never stopped — the house has been counting for thirty years. He photographs Wren; the image shows only an empty chair. Emotional beat: denial cracking; the first proof that Wren isn't human.

chapters.title: The Ledgers
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. In the study he finds surveyors' reports dating back to 1890, each in a different hand, each ending mid-sentence. Every author describes the same boy on the porch. The final entry is signed with a child's handwriting he recognizes as his own, aged seven. Emotional beat: horror of implication — he has been here before.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Fragmented memories surface: a dare at seven years old, a chalk circle on the porch, words spoken aloud to something listening. He invited Wren in — or invited the thing wearing Wren. The house's temperature drops; doors begin opening ahead of him. Emotional beat: guilt as engine of terror.

chapters.title: Wren's Version
chapters.summary: POV Wren (first time). Wren narrates from inside the house's walls, where he waits between vessels. He remembers being a farmhand's son in 1911, taken by the family as the first 'friend.' He loves Xanthe genuinely — which makes his role worse. Emotional beat: tenderness poisoned by complicity; Wren wants to be saved and to save himself.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Night falls fully; the moon swells amber. The house rearranges — exits gone, windows showing only interior rooms. Wren appears at his elbow: 'It rises tonight. You have until sunrise to finish your report.' Emotional beat: claustrophobia; the deadline made cosmic.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms That Aren't There
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe surveys rooms that appear only when measured: a nursery, a chapel, a room lined with coats belonging to every missing surveyor. Each coat pocket holds a finished appraisal — all describing him, arriving tonight. Emotional beat: fatalism; the documentation now documents his doom.

chapters.title: The Founding Family
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe, interleaved with ledger excerpts. He reconstructs the Eastwicks' history — his own ancestors — who bound a hungry presence into the house and fed it a surveyor each harvest moon to keep their name prosperous. His invitation at seven wasn't accident; it was inheritance. Emotional beat: identity collapse; he is both victim and bloodline.

chapters.title: Counting
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren hides Xanthe in the walls during the moon's zenith, whispering the old counting rhyme to mask his heartbeat from the thing moving through the halls — vast, jointed, patient, wearing the sound of Xanthe's mother calling him home. Emotional beat: intimacy under terror; Wren's protection costs him something.

chapters.title: The Rewritten Notes
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe discovers his own field notes have been altered overnight: entries now describe him welcoming the entity gladly. The house edits documentation; his one weapon is being turned against him. He begins writing in code only he can parse. Emotional beat: paranoia; the war over what counts as true.

chapters.title: A Door That Opens Outward
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. A false exit leads to a perfect replica of his childhood street, complete with a seven-year-old version of himself playing with Wren. Walking through it means surrendering the present. He burns the replica down with a surveyor's flare and watches his childhood scream. Emotional beat: severance; choosing the damaged present over the seductive past.

chapters.title: Wren Confesses
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren admits the mechanism: whoever completes the appraisal becomes the house's keeper, bound until they find a replacement. He has lured every surveyor hoping one would finish the paperwork and free him. He chose Xanthe out of love, which is indistinguishable from betrayal. Emotional beat: heartbreak; love as predation.

chapters.title: The Terms of the Deed
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe finds the original covenant hidden in the chimney: the house can be claimed, not escaped. Claim it, and the harvest ends — but you keep the house, and the house keeps you. Sunrise approaches; the entity grows bolder, speaking in his own voice through the vents. Emotional beat: grim clarity; there is no clean way out.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. The entity finally shows itself — a tall absence shaped like everyone Xanthe has lost — and offers a bargain: walk out now, forget again, and it will wait for the next surveyor. It has done this before; forgetting is its oldest trick. Emotional beat: temptation; power offered precisely because accepting corrupts.

chapters.title: The Last Measurement
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe measures the house one final time, room by room, naming each space aloud — reclaiming them by attention alone. Documentation as prayer, as exorcism. The walls resist; Wren holds doors shut against the entity, unraveling as he spends himself. Emotional beat: resolve; devotion as weapon.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Wren. As dawn greys the windows, the entity makes its last play: it offers Wren Xanthe's body and Xanthe's freedom, if Wren stops holding the door. Wren refuses — the first refusal in a century of vessels — and begins to burn away like paper. Emotional beat: sacrifice; the imaginary friend choosing to be real for one moment.

chapters.title: Signature
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. At first light Xanthe signs the deed: his full name, his blood-inked thumbprint, witnessed by Wren's fading handprint. The house goes still. The entity is bound into the completed appraisal — filed, catalogued, contained. Wren dissolves saying 'you counted right this time.' Emotional beat: catharsis through cost.

chapters.title: Keeper
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Weeks later: Xanthe lives at Hollowmere, its official owner, unable to leave past the property line. He maintains the ledgers, adds his own volume, and feels the house breathing easier around him. Power hasn't corrupted him yet — but he catches himself reading the next harvest moon's date with something like anticipation. Emotional beat: uneasy peace; corruption deferred, not denied.

chapters.title: The Next Appraisal Order
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. A letter arrives: a young surveyor has been assigned to assist at Hollowmere. Xanthe recognizes the handwriting style — eager, meticulous, doomed. He understands now what the house expects of a keeper, and what he might become if he opens the gate. Emotional beat: dread reborn; the cycle offering itself to him.

chapters.title: Freya and the Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe, closing on Wren's voice within the walls. Xanthe burns the assistant's assignment letter and instead writes a hymn into the ledger — a song of names, his ancestors', his own, Wren's — sung nightly to keep the entity asleep without feeding it. The last line reveals Freya, the founding matriarch, still humming somewhere below. Emotional beat: vigilance as love; the story ends mid-watch, lamp lit, counting.
